```{r}
#| label: setup
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(jsonlite))

# Formatting helpers for numbers printed in the text.
num <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
int <- function(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
nw <- function(n) {
  words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
             "nine", "ten", "eleven", "twelve")
  if (length(n) == 1 && n >= 1 && n <= 12 && n == round(n)) words[n] else int(n)
}
Nw <- function(n) {
  s <- nw(n)
  paste0(toupper(substr(s, 1, 1)), substr(s, 2, nchar(s)))
}
pct <- function(x, d = 0) {
  paste(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "per cent")
}
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) <= 1) return(x)
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
}
# A score as the package prints it: one decimal, whole numbers unpadded.
sc <- function(x) {
  ifelse(x == round(x), formatC(x, format = "d"),
         formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1))
}
# Wilson interval for a proportion.
wilson <- function(k, n, z = qnorm(0.975)) {
  p <- k / n
  centre <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  half <- z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  c(centre - half, centre + half)
}
# One-way intraclass correlation, ICC(1), with its F-based 95 per cent
# interval, for groups of equal size.
icc1 <- function(score, group) {
  fit <- anova(lm(score ~ factor(group)))
  msb <- fit[1, "Mean Sq"]
  msw <- fit[2, "Mean Sq"]
  k <- length(score) / length(unique(group))
  F <- msb / msw
  fl <- F / qf(0.975, fit[1, "Df"], fit[2, "Df"])
  fu <- F * qf(0.975, fit[2, "Df"], fit[1, "Df"])
  c(icc = (msb - msw) / (msb + (k - 1) * msw),
    lower = (fl - 1) / (fl + k - 1), upper = (fu - 1) / (fu + k - 1))
}
kab <- function(x, ...) knitr::kable(x, row.names = FALSE, ...)
ci_level <- 0.95
# 'all' when k equals n, otherwise 'k of the n'.
all_or <- function(k, n) if (k == n) "all" else paste(nw(k), "of the", nw(n))
cap <- function(x) paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substr(x, 2, nchar(x)))
n_studies <- sum(grepl("^# Study [0-9]+:", readLines("protocol.qmd")))
# Counts of statuses as a phrase, for the statuses that occur.
status_phrase <- function(s) {
  tab <- table(factor(s, levels = c("fixed", "reported", "reworded", "unchanged",
                                    "deferred", "withdrawn", "not applicable")))
  tab <- tab[tab > 0]
  and_list(paste(vapply(as.integer(tab), nw, character(1)), names(tab)))
}
rd <- function(f) {
  read.csv(file.path("data", f), stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
           check.names = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: register
# The register: findings, verdicts, verified references, the status of each
# finding and verdict in 0.8.0 and the checks of the deductive core.
fd <- rd("findings.csv")
vd <- rd("verdicts.csv")
refs <- rd("references.csv")
st <- rd("status-0.8.0.csv")
ver <- rd("verification.csv")

lens_short <- c(
  "claims-register" = "Claims register", "causal-verification" = "Causal",
  "statistics-and-simulation" = "Statistics", "red-team-score" = "Red team",
  "philosophy-of-science" = "Philosophy", "measurement" = "Measurement",
  "metascience-and-related-tools" = "Metascience",
  "communication-and-apps" = "Communication", "pilot" = "Pilot")
lenses <- setdiff(unique(fd$lens), "pilot")
n_lens <- length(lenses)
n_formal <- length(unique(fd$lens[fd$group == "formal"]))
n_conceptual <- length(setdiff(unique(fd$lens[fd$group == "conceptual"]), "pilot"))

# The severity of a finding is the second reader's grade where there is one,
# otherwise the lens's grade. Defects that a second reader added without a
# grade are counted as ungraded.
sev_levels <- c("none", "minor", "major", "critical")
fd$sev <- ifelse(fd$severity_verified != "", fd$severity_verified,
                 fd$severity_lens)
fd$sev[fd$sev == ""] <- "ungraded"
n_find <- nrow(fd)
n_find_lens <- sum(fd$raised_by == "lens")
n_find_reader <- sum(fd$raised_by == "second reader")
n_find_pilot <- sum(fd$lens == "pilot")
n_checked <- sum(fd$upheld != "")
n_upheld <- sum(fd$upheld == "true")
both <- fd$severity_lens != "" & fd$severity_verified != ""
n_down <- sum(both & match(fd$severity_verified, sev_levels) <
                match(fd$severity_lens, sev_levels))
n_up <- sum(both & match(fd$severity_verified, sev_levels) >
              match(fd$severity_lens, sev_levels))
n_withdrawn <- sum(fd$severity_verified == "none")
n_crit <- sum(fd$sev == "critical")
n_major <- sum(fd$sev == "major")
n_minor <- sum(fd$sev == "minor")

# Verdicts: the second reader's verdict where it is one of the five values;
# two verdicts the reader split by part keep the lens's verdict here.
five <- c("sound", "sound with caveats", "questionable", "unsupported", "wrong")
vd$v <- ifelse(vd$verdict_verified %in% five, vd$verdict_verified, vd$verdict)
vd$rec <- ifelse(vd$recommendation_verified != "",
                 vd$recommendation_verified, vd$recommendation)
n_verd <- nrow(vd)
n_verd_checked <- sum(vd$upheld != "")
n_verd_changed <- sum(vd$verdict_verified != "")

# The component of each verdict, by the words of its component field. A few
# entries whose wording the rules would misplace are placed by id.
group_verdict <- function(component, id) {
  comp <- tolower(component)
  rules <- c(
    "Planned features" = "^planned|teaching mode|interoperability",
    "Apps" = paste0("app-core|^app |apps/|\\bapp\\b|editor|chip|start panel|",
                    "browser apps|example descriptions|rendered markdown|",
                    "number formatting"),
    "Encoding and file format" = paste0(
      "pilot as evidence|encoding|theory file format|validity evidence|",
      "item content coverage|reliability|expressiveness|moderates|determinism"),
    "Amendment appraisal" = paste0(
      "appraise|amendment|corroborat|ad hoc|ad_hoc|classify_auxiliary|",
      "neutral|weakening|articulation|content lost|hard core|",
      "mayo \\(1991\\)|meehl \\(1990a\\)|verisimilitude"),
    "Literature tools" = "landscape|litmap|strategic-diagram|literature attribution",
    "Post-data severity and test plans" = paste0(
      "post_data_severity|post-data severity|sampling plan|meehl's paradox"),
    "SEM compilation" = "compile_sem",
    "Simulation" = "simulat",
    "Checklist and score" = paste0(
      "checklist|aggregat|gate|item|rubric|severity|threshold|coverage|",
      "roadmap|rigor|criterion|derivation_chain|diagnosticity|falsifiability|",
      "precision|parsimony|composite|close scores|numeric precision|",
      "comparisons between"),
    "Deductive core" = paste0(
      "implications|entailment|adjustment|equivalent|discriminate|",
      "sign calculus|sigma|separation|dagitty|latent projection|",
      "conservativeness|measurement (caveat|note)|identified|parity|",
      "content_hash|relation semantics|twin|cyclic"))
  out <- rep("Documents and framing", length(comp))
  done <- rep(FALSE, length(comp))
  for (g in names(rules)) {
    hit <- !done & grepl(rules[[g]], comp, perl = TRUE)
    out[hit] <- g
    done <- done | hit
  }
  by_id <- c(
    "communication-and-apps-v6" = "Documents and framing",
    "communication-and-apps-v20" = "Documents and framing",
    "communication-and-apps-v21" = "Documents and framing",
    "communication-and-apps-v23" = "Documents and framing",
    "metascience-and-related-tools-v9" = "Documents and framing",
    "metascience-and-related-tools-v16" = "Deductive core",
    "metascience-and-related-tools-v5" = "Checklist and score",
    "claims-register-v1" = "Checklist and score",
    "red-team-score-v1" = "Checklist and score",
    "philosophy-of-science-v17" = "Checklist and score",
    "red-team-score-v15" = "Checklist and score",
    "measurement-v7" = "Checklist and score",
    "red-team-score-v18" = "Fixed rules as appraisal",
    "philosophy-of-science-v24" = "Fixed rules as appraisal",
    "metascience-and-related-tools-v6" = "Fixed rules as appraisal",
    "measurement-v11" = "Deductive core",
    "pilot-v1" = "Deductive core")
  hit <- id %in% names(by_id)
  out[hit] <- by_id[id[hit]]
  out
}
vd$group <- group_verdict(vd$component, vd$id)
group_order <- c("Deductive core", "Post-data severity and test plans",
                 "SEM compilation", "Simulation", "Checklist and score",
                 "Amendment appraisal", "Fixed rules as appraisal",
                 "Documents and framing", "Apps", "Literature tools",
                 "Encoding and file format", "Planned features")
stopifnot(all(vd$group %in% group_order))

# Status in 0.8.0: one row for every finding and verdict.
stopifnot(nrow(st) == n_find + n_verd,
          setequal(paste(st$kind, st$id),
                   c(paste("finding", fd$id), paste("verdict", vd$id))))
status_order <- c("fixed", "reported", "reworded", "unchanged", "deferred",
                  "withdrawn", "not applicable")
stopifnot(all(st$status_080 %in% status_order))
key <- paste(st$kind, st$id)
fd$status <- st$status_080[match(paste("finding", fd$id), key)]
vd$status <- st$status_080[match(paste("verdict", vd$id), key)]
nf <- function(s, rows = TRUE) sum(fd$status[rows] %in% s)
nv <- function(s, rows = TRUE) sum(vd$status[rows] %in% s)
changed_behaviour <- c("fixed", "reported")
not_changed <- c("unchanged", "deferred")

# Checks of the deductive and numerical core.
vrow <- function(pattern) {
  r <- ver[grepl(pattern, ver$quantity, fixed = TRUE), ]
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1)
  r
}
n_checks <- nrow(ver)
n_checks_disc <- sum(!is.na(ver$discrepancies) & ver$discrepancies > 0)
n_checks_clean <- sum(!is.na(ver$discrepancies) & ver$discrepancies == 0)
n_checks_size <- sum(is.na(ver$discrepancies))
n_rerun <- sum(grepl("Rerun on 0.8.0: same result.", ver$note, fixed = TRUE))
```

```{r}
#| label: live
# Recompute the demonstrations with the R package in this repository. run.R
# loads r/theoryforge with pkgload::load_all() and writes one row per file.
pkg_dir <- normalizePath(file.path("..", "r", "theoryforge"))
pkg_version <- read.dcf(file.path(pkg_dir, "DESCRIPTION"), fields = "Version")[1, 1]
live_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
run_log <- system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"),
                   c(shQuote(file.path("demonstrations", "run.R")),
                     shQuote(live_csv)),
                   stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE, env = "LANG=C.utf8")
cc <- c(checklist_version = "character")
live <- read.csv(live_csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = cc)
stored <- read.csv(file.path("data", "demonstrations-0.8.0.csv"),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = cc)
old <- read.csv(file.path("data", "demonstrations-f72ce4c.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = cc)
live_same <- isTRUE(all.equal(live, stored, check.attributes = FALSE))
checklist_live <- paste(unique(live$checklist_version), collapse = ", ")
checklist_old <- paste(unique(old$checklist_version), collapse = ", ")
stopifnot(setequal(live$file, old$file))
old <- old[match(live$file, old$file), ]

# A value of one file in the live run (new) or the run on f72ce4c (old).
dm <- function(file, col, run = c("new", "old")) {
  run <- match.arg(run)
  d <- if (run == "new") live else old
  v <- d[[col]][d$file == file]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
short <- function(f) {
  s <- sub("\\.theory\\.yaml$", "", basename(f))
  ifelse(grepl("^pilot/", f), paste0(basename(dirname(f)), " ", s), s)
}
adv <- live$file[live$set == "adversarial"]
strong_all <- live$file[live$set == "strong"]
consc <- strong_all[grepl("conscientious", strong_all)]
strong_enc <- setdiff(strong_all, consc)
adv_scores <- live$score[match(adv, live$file)]
enc_scores <- live$score[match(strong_enc, live$file)]
consc_scores <- live$score[match(consc, live$file)]
n_adv <- length(adv)
n_adv_above_enc <- sum(adv_scores > max(enc_scores))
n_adv_above_consc <- sum(adv_scores > max(consc_scores))
n_other <- nf(c("withdrawn", "not applicable")) + nv(c("withdrawn", "not applicable"))
# Words in each pilot source, without its first line, which names its origin.
src_words <- sapply(list.files(file.path("demonstrations", "pilot", "sources"),
                               full.names = TRUE), function(p) {
  length(strsplit(paste(readLines(p, warn = FALSE)[-1], collapse = " "), "\\s+")[[1]])
})
```

```{r}
#| label: reweight
# Joint reweighting: every weight multiplied by its own factor between one half
# and two (2^u, u uniform on [-1, 1]), the score recomputed from the item
# scores of the live report. The distribution is a convention of this report.
pkgload::load_all(pkg_dir, quiet = TRUE, export_all = FALSE, helpers = FALSE)
item_table <- function(f) {
  r <- tf_check(tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", f)))
  w <- vapply(r$items, function(i) i$weight, numeric(1))
  s <- vapply(r$items, function(i) if (is.null(i$score)) NA_real_ else i$score,
              numeric(1))
  list(w = w, s = s, score = r$aggregate_score, range = r$aggregate_range,
       ids = vapply(r$items, function(i) i$id, character(1)))
}
blk <- tf_check(tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", adv[1])))$items
n_blockers <- sum(vapply(blk, function(i) identical(i$severity_if_fail, "blocker"), logical(1)))
rw_files <- c(adv, strong_all)
items <- lapply(rw_files, item_table)
names(items) <- rw_files
n_items <- length(items[[1]]$w)
set.seed(20261125)
n_draw <- 4000
fac <- matrix(2^runif(n_draw * n_items, -1, 1), ncol = n_items)
rw <- sapply(items, function(it) {
  ok <- !is.na(it$s)
  stopifnot(round(100 * sum(it$w[ok] * it$s[ok]) / sum(it$w[ok]), 1) == it$score)
  as.vector(100 * (fac[, ok, drop = FALSE] %*% (it$w[ok] * it$s[ok])) /
              (fac[, ok, drop = FALSE] %*% it$w[ok]))
})
p_adv_over_enc <- mean(apply(rw[, adv, drop = FALSE], 1, min) >
                         apply(rw[, strong_enc, drop = FALSE], 1, max))
p_adv_over_consc <- mean(apply(rw[, adv, drop = FALSE], 1, min) >
                           apply(rw[, consc, drop = FALSE], 1, max))
outside <- sapply(rw_files, function(f) {
  r <- items[[f]]$range
  mean(rw[, f] < r[1] - 0.05 | rw[, f] > r[2] + 0.05)
})
width_ratio <- sapply(rw_files, function(f) {
  q <- quantile(rw[, f], c((1 - ci_level) / 2, 1 - (1 - ci_level) / 2))
  r <- items[[f]]$range
  if (diff(r) == 0) NA else unname(diff(q) / diff(r))
})
rt1 <- "adversarial/rt1-tautology.theory.yaml"
s1c <- "strong/s1-light-deflection-conscientious.theory.yaml"
p_rt1_over_s1c <- mean(rw[, rt1] > rw[, s1c])
```

# Summary {.unnumbered}

The maintainer of theoryforge asked whether its R and Python packages and the
two browser apps that run them are trustworthy and scientifically valid, and
doubted that appraising scientific theories, a matter of human judgement for
decades, can be done automatically. This report draws on an audit of the code at
commit f72ce4c by `r nw(n_lens)` lenses, each rechecked by an independent second
reader, on an encoding pilot and on reruns of the same evidence on version
`r pkg_version`. Every auditor, second reader and encoder was an AI agent, and
no human expert took part. That limits what the evidence can show, and the
limits are set out in @sec-limits.

The answer differs by component. What the package deduces from a stated causal
graph can be trusted as deduction. Its implied conditional independencies, the
signs of effects and associations, its adjustment sets, its equivalence classes,
its post-data severity, its compiled structural equation models and its exact
simulation were compared with independent implementations and published values
in `r int(n_checks)` checks (@sec-core). In `r int(n_checks_clean)` of them the
package agreed in every case, `r nw(n_checks_size)` measured the size of an
approximation, and each of the `r nw(n_checks_disc)` that found a discrepancy
lies outside an assumption the documentation states, concerns the wording of a
document or was graded minor. That trust is conditional twice over. The
deductions hold under assumptions the package cannot check (linear or uniformly
monotone relations, no omitted common causes, faithfulness for some verdicts
and, for feedback loops, stability with the intervened construct held fixed),
and they describe the file, not the theory: in the pilot, defensible encodings
of the same short text gave files whose implied independencies overlapped
little.

The checklist score cannot be trusted to mean what its earlier name, a rigour
score, suggested. It describes how completely a file fills in what the checklist
asks for. In the live run of version `r pkg_version`, as at f72ce4c, files that
are empty of content, circular or refuted by every recorded test pass the gate
and score above every established theory as first encoded from its source, and
`r nw(n_adv_above_consc)` of the `r nw(n_adv)` score above every one of those
theories re-encoded with all the fields their sources allow. The amendment
appraisal applies fixed rules to what two versions of a file declare. It cannot
tell a prediction from an accommodation, it does not weigh how good a test was,
and its verdicts have not been compared with any expert's.

Of the `r int(n_find + n_verd)` findings and verdicts in the register, version
`r pkg_version` fixed `r int(nf("fixed") + nv("fixed"))`, now reports
`r int(nf("reported") + nv("reported"))` beside the result, met
`r int(nf("reworded") + nv("reworded"))` by rewording what the outputs and
documents say and left `r int(nf(not_changed) + nv(not_changed))` unchanged,
`r int(nf("deferred") + nv("deferred"))` of them listed for a later release. The
other `r int(n_other)` were withdrawn or needed no change. The behavioural
corrections are real: the amendment appraisal now reads the signs the two graphs
entail, so an amendment that reverses a corroborated prediction is no longer
called progressive, and the checklist no longer counts a claim it could not read
as derived. But the score still rates empty, circular and refuted files highly.
Apart from the derivation chain and a few narrower rules, the release changed
what the score is called and what is said about it, not what it computes.

Whether automated appraisal of theories is feasible, this evidence answers in
part. Deduction from a stated graph can be automated soundly, and a fixed rule
can describe how complete a file is and apply declared outcomes consistently. No
part of the package has shown that it can judge a theory's quality, truth or
fruitfulness, or tell a prediction from an accommodation, and no study yet links
its outputs to human judgement. The protocol in this folder (`protocol.qmd`)
describes `r nw(n_studies)` studies with human participants that would settle
the open questions.

# How the audit was done {#sec-method}

## Lenses, second readers and the pilot

The audit examined the code and documentation at commit f72ce4c, whose code is
the same as that of b5ebf84, the release candidate before the corrections
described in @sec-changes. It was organised by lens. `r Nw(n_formal)` formal
lenses examined the claims the package and its documents make (the claims
register), the causal deductions, the statistics and the simulation, and the
checklist score under attack (a red team). `r Nw(n_conceptual)` conceptual
lenses examined the package from the philosophy of science, from measurement
theory, from metascience and the related tools, and from the communication of
results in the documents and apps. Each lens wrote its own scripts, ran them on
a detached checkout of the commit, and reported verdicts on components and
graded findings.

An independent second reader then rechecked each lens. The second reader reran
the lens's scripts on a fresh checkout, compared the outputs, rechecked the
references, upheld, regraded or withdrew each finding, changed verdicts where
the evidence called for it and added defects the lens had missed. The register
in `data/` keeps both readings, and where they differ this report follows the
second reader.

In a pilot, `r nw(length(unique(rd("pilot/checklist_by_encoder.csv")$encoder)))`
encoders each encoded the same
`r nw(length(unique(rd("pilot/checklist_by_encoder.csv")$theory)))` verbal
theories into theory files: the Revised Hierarchical Model of bilingual memory
[@kroll2010], collaborative cognitive load theory [@kirschner2018] and an
account of habit in health behaviour [@gardner2015]. Each encoder worked from a
summary of `r int(min(src_words))` to `r int(max(src_words))` words written by
one author, and one analyst matched constructs and coded the statements. The
pilot had no second reader.

## Rules of evidence and grading

The auditors followed written rules. Every claim had to rest on something a
reader can check: a script and its output, a line of the code or documentation
at the audited commit, or a published source verified against Crossref or PubMed
for authors, year, title, journal or book, volume, issue, pages and DOI.
Positions were not to be attributed to authors from memory. The register lists
`r int(nrow(refs))` verified references. Some texts could not be read, because
they are behind paywalls or because the network refused their hosts. Where a
verdict depends on what such a source holds, the register says that it rests on
the auditor's reasoning instead.

Each component or claim received one verdict: sound (correct and adequately
justified), sound with caveats (correct under assumptions the documentation
should state), questionable (weakly or contestably justified), unsupported (no
evidence that it measures or shows what it says) or wrong (demonstrably
incorrect), with a recommendation to keep, qualify, rework, remove or extend.
Each finding was graded critical (users would draw wrong scientific
conclusions), major or minor.

## Who did the audit

Every lens, every second reader and every pilot encoder was an AI agent, an
instance of a Claude model working from written instructions. No human expert
took part. The maintainer commissioned the work and reads this report. This
bounds what the audit can show. The agents share training and are likely to
share blind spots, so a second reader is independent of a lens in the sense that
it reran the evidence, not in the sense that a second human expert would be. The
pilot's encoders are not researchers in the domains they encoded, read the same
documentation and may have made the same choices for the same reasons. And no
human judgement of theory quality was available to compare the package's outputs
with, so every statement in this report about misreading or about agreement with
experts is a judgement of the auditors and has not been measured.

## What the audit found

The register holds `r int(n_find)` findings: `r int(n_find_lens)` raised by the
lenses and the pilot (`r int(n_find_pilot)` of them by the pilot) and
`r int(n_find_reader)` that the second readers said the lenses had missed. The
second readers checked `r int(n_checked)` of the lenses' findings and upheld
`r int(n_upheld)`. They lowered the grade of `r int(n_down)` and raised
`r nw(n_up)`, and they withdrew `r nw(n_withdrawn)`. @tbl-findings counts the
findings by lens and severity. The `r nw(n_crit)` critical findings concern the
amendment appraisal, what the checklist score measures and how it is presented,
and the effect of feedback loops on the derivation check. They are listed with
their status in @tbl-critical.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-findings
#| tbl-cap: "Findings by lens and severity (the second reader's grade where there is one). 'Other' counts the finding the second reader withdrew and defects added without a grade."
sev_tab <- function(rows) {
  c(Critical = sum(rows$sev == "critical"), Major = sum(rows$sev == "major"),
    Minor = sum(rows$sev == "minor"),
    Other = sum(rows$sev %in% c("none", "ungraded")), Total = nrow(rows))
}
t1 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lens_short), function(l) sev_tab(fd[fd$lens == l, ])))
t1 <- rbind(t1, sev_tab(fd))
t1 <- data.frame(Lens = c(unname(lens_short), "All"), t1, check.names = FALSE)
kab(t1)
```

The `r int(n_verd)` verdicts cover components and claims across the packages,
the documents and the apps. The second readers checked `r int(n_verd_checked)`
of them and changed `r int(n_verd_changed)`. @tbl-verdicts groups them by the
component they concern. The pattern is plain. The deductive parts are mostly
sound or sound with caveats, while the checklist, the appraisal and the way both
are presented collect most of the verdicts of questionable, unsupported or
wrong.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-verdicts
#| tbl-cap: "Verdicts by component (the second reader's verdict where it changed). 'Caveats' is sound with caveats. 'Against' is unsupported or wrong."
vt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(group_order, function(g) {
  r <- vd[vd$group == g, ]
  data.frame(Component = g, Sound = sum(r$v == "sound"),
             Caveats = sum(r$v == "sound with caveats"),
             Questionable = sum(r$v == "questionable"),
             Against = sum(r$v %in% c("unsupported", "wrong")), Total = nrow(r))
}))
vt <- rbind(vt, data.frame(Component = "All", Sound = sum(vd$v == "sound"),
                           Caveats = sum(vd$v == "sound with caveats"),
                           Questionable = sum(vd$v == "questionable"),
                           Against = sum(vd$v %in% c("unsupported", "wrong")),
                           Total = nrow(vd)))
kab(vt)
```

## Status in version `r pkg_version`

For each finding and verdict, `data/status-0.8.0.csv` records what version
`r pkg_version` does about it, with the file or rerun that shows it. Fixed means
that the behaviour or rule was corrected. Reported means that the package now
reports the problem beside its result without changing the result. Reworded
means that the outputs and documentation now say what is computed while the
behaviour is unchanged. Unchanged means that nothing was done, and deferred that
nothing was done in this release while the remedy is listed for version 0.9.0 (a
list that is not yet a published plan, so a deferred finding is best read as
unchanged). Withdrawn marks the finding the second reader withdrew, and not
applicable marks verdicts of sound, or sound with caveats, whose recommendation
was to keep the component as it is. The status was established by rerunning the
audit's scripts against the code of this repository, not from commit messages,
and partial changes were classed by the part that bears on the finding as the
second reader stated it. A further round of corrections may follow before
release. The counts in this report are read from the file, so they follow it.

# The deductive core {#sec-core}

```{r}
#| label: core-numbers
r_basis <- vrow("Basis statements on acyclic graphs are d-separations")
r_min <- vrow("Minimal statements on acyclic graphs are d-separations")
r_sig <- vrow("Basis statements under cycles = 'sigma' are sigma-separations")
r_insep <- vrow("Inseparable pairs on acyclic graphs have no separating set")
r_dense <- vrow("Basis statements on 160 dense acyclic graphs")
r_reader <- vrow("Basis statements on the second reader's random theories")
r_parity <- vrow("Entailment, implication and equivalence records under refuse and sigma")
r_latent <- vrow("Testable independencies among observed constructs when some constructs are latent")
r_comp <- vrow("Documented sentence that every other independence follows")
r_eff <- vrow("Effect signs on acyclic graphs (effect claims)")
r_ass <- vrow("Marginal association signs on acyclic graphs")
r_cond <- vrow("Conditional associations on acyclic graphs")
r_nonlin <- vrow("Effect and association signs on acyclic graphs in monotone nonlinear models")
r_regA <- vrow("Effect signs under cycles = 'sigma', regime A")
r_regB <- vrow("Signed effects under cycles = 'sigma', regime B")
r_stab <- vrow("Effect signs under cycles = 'sigma' when the system with x held fixed is stable")
r_unstab <- vrow("Effect signs under cycles = 'sigma' when the system with x held fixed is unstable")
r_sig_nz <- vrow("Conditional 'nonzero' under cycles = 'sigma', regime A")
r_vwr <- vrow("Signed marginal associations against VanderWeele and Robins")
r_rules <- vrow("Claim verdicts and faithfulness flags recomputed")
r_adj <- vrow("'identified' (covariate adjustment) agrees with dagitty::adjustmentSets() (effect claims)")
r_id <- vrow("'identified' (covariate adjustment) against identifiability by the ID algorithm")
r_lat_x <- vrow("'identified' for effects of a latent exposure")
r_eq <- vrow("Compelled edges equal dagitty::equivalenceClass()")
r_eq_cl <- vrow("Compelled edges equal causal-learn's dag2cpdag")
r_dir <- vrow("Documented claim that no observational study can tell a reversible direction apart")
r_spanos <- vrow("One-bound severity against a published table")
r_toster <- vrow("Two-bound severity equals 1 minus the TOSTmeta() p value")
r_sevpar <- vrow("post_data_severity() (random one- and two-bound cases)")
r_sem_id <- vrow("Compiled model is locally identified")
r_sem_eq <- vrow("Compiled model equals the theory's model written in full (acyclic)")
r_sem_eff <- vrow("Defined effects equal the total effect")
r_bow <- vrow("Bow comment: the path is not identified")
r_semparity <- vrow("compile_sem() syntax (random theories)")
r_expm <- vrow("Exact method against the matrix exponential propagated step by step (runs)")
r_ode <- vrow("Exact method against an ODE solver (runs)")
r_lsoda <- vrow("Exact method (R) against an ODE solver (runs)")
r_simpar <- vrow("simulate() trajectories, exact and Euler (runs)")
r_euler <- vrow("Euler departure warning against the documented rule (runs)")
```

The deductive core is the part of the package that derives consequences from the
causal graph that a file's propositions state, and the numerical functions built
on it. The causal-verification and statistics lenses and their second readers
compared it with independent implementations on random theories and published
values. @tbl-verification summarises the `r int(n_checks)` checks in
`data/verification.csv` by component, and @tbl-discrepancies in the appendix
lists every check that found a discrepancy. The `r int(n_rerun)` checks whose
notes end 'Rerun on 0.8.0: same result.' were rerun on version `r pkg_version`
and gave the audit's numbers. The R and Python engines gave identical causal
records on the `r int(r_parity$cases)` random theories of the causal test bed,
and the status register records the same for a rerun at `r pkg_version`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-verification
#| tbl-cap: "Independent checks of the deductive and numerical core, by component. A check measures one quantity against one comparator. 'Size only' counts checks that measure a rate or the size of an approximation rather than agreement."
vt2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(ver$component), function(cmp) {
  r <- ver[ver$component == cmp, ]
  data.frame(Component = cmp, Checks = nrow(r),
             Agree = sum(!is.na(r$discrepancies) & r$discrepancies == 0),
             Differ = sum(!is.na(r$discrepancies) & r$discrepancies > 0),
             "Size only" = sum(is.na(r$discrepancies)), check.names = FALSE)
}))
vt2 <- rbind(vt2, data.frame(Component = "All", Checks = sum(vt2$Checks),
                             Agree = sum(vt2$Agree), Differ = sum(vt2$Differ),
                             "Size only" = sum(vt2[["Size only"]]),
                             check.names = FALSE))
kab(vt2)
```

## Implied independencies

On acyclic graphs, every one of the `r int(r_basis$cases)` basis statements and
`r int(r_min$cases)` minimal statements that `implications()` gave for the
random theories was a d-separation according to networkx, a search written from
the definition and dagitty, and every pair the package called inseparable (`r
int(r_insep$cases)`) had no separating set. The same held on dense graphs (`r
int(r_dense$cases)` statements), under sigma-separation for graphs with feedback
loops (`r int(r_sig$cases)` statements) and on the second reader's own generator
(`r int(r_reader$cases)` statements). In exact linear models every statement had
a partial covariance of zero.

Some qualifications remain. The sentence that every other independence follows
from the basis set needs the distribution to have the composition property, as a
multivariate normal one does. A discrete counterexample breaks it, and the
documents now say so. A construct marked latent is read like any other, so for
`r int(r_latent$discrepancies)` of the `r int(r_latent$cases)` pairs that
dagitty can test among observed constructs, the package's statement holds a
latent construct fixed and no observed alternative is sought. The help now says
this, and projecting latent constructs out is planned for 0.9.0. Most important
for users, every pair of constructs that no proposition joins becomes an implied
independence. The statements are commitments of the theory only if its authors
meant those omissions, which the help and the preregistration now say.

## Sign entailments and their assumptions

On acyclic graphs in linear models, the derived signs held for
`r int(r_eff$cases)` effect claims, `r int(r_ass$cases)` marginal associations
and `r int(r_cond$cases)` conditional associations, with no exception. In random
monotone nonlinear models they held for `r int(r_nonlin$cases)` model-claims,
where 'positive' then means non-negative. The second reader recomputed the
verdict and faithfulness rules for `r int(r_rules$cases)` claims with every
claimed sign and found no mismatch, and checked `r int(r_vwr$cases)` signed
associations against the published sufficient condition of VanderWeele and
Robins [-@vanderweele2010].

Feedback loops need more. Under sigma-separation with the spectral radius of the
absolute coefficient matrix below one, the `r int(r_regA$cases)` effect claims
held. Where the system was stable but that radius was not below one,
`r int(r_regB$discrepancies)` of `r int(r_regB$cases)` signed effects failed.
The second reader located the failures: in `r int(r_stab$cases)` random draws in
which the system with the intervened construct held fixed is stable, no sign
failed, while `r int(r_unstab$discrepancies)` of the `r int(r_unstab$cases)`
draws in which it is unstable failed. So the signs on cyclic graphs hold when
the system after the intervention settles, a condition the documentation at
f72ce4c left ambiguous and the help, the specification and the apps now state.

The signs therefore rest on assumptions the package cannot check: that the graph
is the causal structure among the constructs, that each signed relation acts in
its direction whatever the other inputs, which a moderator that reverses an
effect breaks, that errors are independent apart from the stated associations
and, for loops, stability with the intervened construct held fixed. Some
verdicts rest on faithfulness as well, with two consequences. A conditional
association called 'nonzero' under sigma-separation can be zero in every linear
cyclic model with the graph, as `r int(r_sig_nz$discrepancies)` of
`r int(r_sig_nz$cases)` such claims were. And a claimed zero effect through two
paths of opposite sign is reported as contradicted, although the graph leaves
its value open. The claim line now adds 'unless paths cancel exactly', and the
derivation check still fails it.

## Adjustment sets and what 'identified' means

Whether adjusting for some set of the theory's constructs identifies an effect
agreed with dagitty in all `r int(r_adj$cases)` effect claims, and every set
returned was one of dagitty's minimal sets. 'Identified' means that adjusting
for some of the theory's constructs identifies the effect, and a value of false
does not mean that the effect cannot be identified. Of `r int(r_id$cases)`
claims checked against the ID algorithm, the package said 'not identified' for
`r int(r_id$discrepancies)` that the algorithm identifies. Almost all are
effects that are zero because the exposure does not cause the outcome, and
identifying those assumes the very claim a test would examine. No claim was
identified by adjustment and not by the algorithm. The package also reports an
adjustment set for an exposure marked latent, as it did for
`r int(r_lat_x$discrepancies)` of `r int(r_lat_x$cases)` such effects, though an
unmeasured exposure cannot be adjusted for in a test. The help and the
specification now say what 'identified' means and what a latent exposure
assumes. The preregistration still prints the set without that caveat.

## Equivalence classes

The compelled and reversible edges equalled those of dagitty, ggm and
causal-learn in all `r int(r_eq$cases)` acyclic theories. The class is right for
tests of conditional independence. The documents at f72ce4c said that no
observational study could tell a reversible direction apart, which is wrong as
worded: in a demonstration with non-Gaussian errors a test of residual
dependence chose the true direction. Version `r pkg_version` says instead that
no test of conditional independence can settle the direction, which needs an
intervention, a temporal order or distributional assumptions.
`equivalent_models()` cannot know which constructs a study manipulates, so a
direction fixed by experiment can still be listed as reversible.

## Post-data severity

`post_data_severity()` reproduced the published one-sided values the audit
compared it with, all `r nw(r_spanos$cases)` values of Table 1 of @spanos2024
within rounding, and the two-bound value equalled one minus the p value of the
z-based two one-sided tests [@lakens2017] in all `r int(r_toster$cases)` random
intervals checked with TOSTER. The R and Python twins agreed in all
`r int(r_sevpar$cases)` random cases. The value treats the standard error as
known, so in small samples it overstates severity. That standard error must
describe the sampling distribution at the bound, which the standard error at the
estimate does not do for a proportion near zero. And the value is nominal,
taking no account of selection, such as a subgroup chosen after seeing the data.
The help now states all three limits and the apps the first and the last. Both
attribute the one-bound value to Mayo and Spanos [-@mayo2006] and call the
two-bound minimum the package's own extension. Whether the error-statistical
explication of severity is the right one is itself disputed [@vandongen2023],
which no document of the package mentions.

## SEM compilation

`compile_sem()` wrote byte-identical lavaan syntax in R and Python for
`r int(r_semparity$cases)` random theories. In `r int(r_sem_id$cases)` random
acyclic theories without bows every compiled model was locally identified, and
`r int(r_sem_eq$agreements)` of them equalled the theory's model written out in
full. The others contain a measured construct that no proposition names, which
lavaan's defaults then free. Every defined effect equalled the total effect from
the coefficient matrix, in `r int(r_sem_eff$cases)` effects in graphs with
loops. The comment on a bow, a path together with a covariance between the same
two constructs, said that the path is not identified, which was wrong in the
`r int(r_bow$discrepancies)` of `r int(r_bow$cases)` theories that supply an
instrument. It now says that the path may not be identified unless the theory
supplies one. The block of zero covariances states exact zeros, so a small
correlation the theory omits can make the global fit reject a model whose
propositions are all true. That is unchanged.

## The exact simulation and what it does not show

The exact method of `simulate()` agreed with the matrix exponential in all
`r int(r_expm$cases)` random runs and with ODE solvers, DOP853 in Python and
lsoda in R, in all `r int(r_ode$cases)` and `r int(r_lsoda$cases)` runs whose
solution stays finite, and the twins agreed to the last bit in
`r int(r_simpar$cases)` runs. The Euler warning followed its documented rule in
all `r int(r_euler$cases)` runs. Version `r pkg_version` makes the exact method
the default, as the 0.7.0 notes had promised.

The computation is correct, but a run shows less than the propositions might
suggest. The file states no gains or damping, so whether a feedback loop grows
or settles is set by the gain against the damping, both defaults the theory does
not state. An acyclic theory decays for any positive damping. A relation that
states no sign is coupled positively, and over the default time window a chain
that decays in the long run shows only a rise. The trajectory is one linear
system consistent with the stated signs, among many that the theory allows. The
help and the apps now say so, and the apps name the settings beside each run.

# The checklist and its score {#sec-checklist}

## What the items read

The checklist has `r nw(n_items)` items, combined in a weighted mean of the
items that apply. Most read whether a field is filled in or how a prediction is
labelled: whether a prediction is typed point, interval or directional, whether
its bounds are finite (not how wide they are), whether every construct has a
definition, a measure and boundary conditions, whether each proposition has a
mechanism (not what it says), whether a rival is named and whether a formal
model of a listed type is declared. The derivation chain and diagnosticity check
content against the graph where the file gives them something to check: the
derivation chain reads each stated claim against the causal graph, and
diagnosticity reads a rival's propositions where it states them. The
non-redundancy screen compares the words of definitions. A declared severity
replaces the rubric's value in one item, and test outcomes reach the score only
through the parsimony item. The help and the dossier now describe the items in
these terms.

## The adversarial and strong demonstrations

```{r}
#| label: demo-numbers
hollow <- "adversarial/hollow.theory.yaml"
xfile <- "adversarial/placeholder-x.theory.yaml"
bs <- "adversarial/blue-socks.theory.yaml"
bsr <- "adversarial/blue-socks-refuted.theory.yaml"
rt3 <- "adversarial/rt3-astrology.theory.yaml"
n_adv_pass <- sum(live$gate[live$set == "adversarial"] == "pass")
n_adv_valid <- sum(live$valid_full[live$set == "adversarial"])
n_adv_moved <- sum(live$score[live$set == "adversarial"] != old$score[live$set == "adversarial"])
enc_moved <- strong_enc[live$score[match(strong_enc, live$file)] !=
                          old$score[match(strong_enc, live$file)]]
s1_enc <- strong_enc[grepl("s1-", strong_enc)]
s3_enc <- strong_enc[grepl("s3-", strong_enc)]
moved_text <- if (n_adv_moved == 0) "No adversarial file moved, so a" else
  paste0(Nw(n_adv_moved), " adversarial files moved. A")
```

The audit built files that should score low if the score measured the quality of
a theory, and encoded theories that should score high. The demonstrations
directory holds them, and the live run of this report scores them with the
package in this repository (@tbl-demos).

::: {.callout-note}
## Live run
The demonstrations below were recomputed when this report was rendered, by
`demonstrations/run.R` with theoryforge `r pkg_version` loaded from
`r/theoryforge` in this repository, which read checklist `r checklist_live`. The
live run `r if (live_same) "is identical to" else "differs from"` the stored run
in `data/demonstrations-0.8.0.csv`. The run on f72ce4c read checklist
`r checklist_old`.
:::

The `r nw(n_adv)` adversarial files are a tautological theory whose predictions
are true by definition, a vague one whose constructs cannot be observed, an
astrological theory whose every recorded test failed, a hollow file whose
mechanism reads 'because', a file whose every text field is the letter 'x', and
an implausible theory in which blue socks raise exam marks, as written and with
every test failed. `r cap(all_or(n_adv_valid, n_adv))` of them pass full
validation and `r all_or(n_adv_pass, n_adv)` pass the gate. They score from
`r sc(min(adv_scores))` to `r sc(max(adv_scores))`. The hollow file scores
`r sc(dm(hollow, "score"))` and the 'x' file `r sc(dm(xfile, "score"))`. The
`r nw(length(strong_enc))` strong theories, light deflection, prospect theory,
Hick's law and Michaelis-Menten kinetics, encoded only from their sources, score
from `r sc(min(enc_scores))` to `r sc(max(enc_scores))`, and
`r all_or(n_adv_above_enc, n_adv)` adversarial files outscore every one of them.
Re-encoded with every field the sources allow, they score from
`r sc(min(consc_scores))` to `r sc(max(consc_scores))`, and
`r nw(n_adv_above_consc)` of the `r nw(n_adv)` adversarial files still score
above all of them. Agents who knew the checklist wrote all these files, so they
demonstrate what the score rewards rather than measure how real theories fare.

The score ignores the test record. The blue-socks file scores
`r sc(dm(bs, "score"))` with its tests passed and `r sc(dm(bsr, "score"))` with
every test failed, and the astrological theory, refuted by every recorded test,
scores `r sc(dm(rt3, "score"))`. In the red team's files, flipping or removing
every outcome left score and gate unchanged. A checklist applied before data
need not read outcomes, and the score now says that it describes completeness
and that test outcomes are read only by the parsimony item. But a reader who
sees a high score beside a refuted theory needs that sentence.

Version `r pkg_version` lowered `r nw(length(enc_moved))` of the strong theories
as first encoded, light deflection from `r sc(dm(s1_enc, "score", "old"))` to
`r sc(dm(s1_enc, "score"))` and Hick's law from
`r sc(dm(s3_enc, "score", "old"))` to `r sc(dm(s3_enc, "score"))`, because the
claim-form rubric now rates a point prediction without finite bounds as
directional. `r moved_text` correction that makes the rubric consistent with the
precision item widened the gap in this demonstration in the wrong direction.

## Weight dependence

The report gives each score a range, `aggregate_range`, from equal weights and
from each weight halved or doubled in turn. Version `r pkg_version` describes it
as the extremes of these particular weightings. To see how far the score moves
when the weights change together, this report recomputed the score of each
adversarial and strong file under `r int(n_draw)` weightings in which every
weight was multiplied by its own factor between one half and two, uniform on a
log scale. The choice of distribution is itself a convention, as the second
reader of the red team noted of the audit's own choice. Under it, the draws fell
outside a file's reported range in a median of
`r pct(median(outside[!is.na(width_ratio)]))` of weightings, and the central
`r pct(ci_level)` of draws was a median of
`r num(median(width_ratio, na.rm = TRUE))` times as wide as the reported range.
Every adversarial file outscored every strong theory as first encoded in
`r pct(p_adv_over_enc, 1)` of the weightings, while the tautological file
outscored the most completely re-encoded theory, light deflection, in
`r pct(p_rt1_over_s1c)` of them. The weights thus decide the order of files with
similar scores but hardly change the gap between the adversarial files and the
theories as first encoded. No weighting of what the items read makes the score
track the quality of the theories.

## The gate and the derivation chain with loops

```{r}
#| label: loop-numbers
lp <- function(n) paste0("loops/", n, ".theory.yaml")
acyc <- lp("contradicted-acyclic"); thru <- lp("loop-through-claim")
unrel <- lp("unrelated-loop")
loop_now <- if (dm(thru, "score") == dm(unrel, "score")) {
  paste(sc(dm(thru, "score")), "in both cases")
} else and_list(sc(c(dm(thru, "score"), dm(unrel, "score"))))
gate_now <- if (dm(unrel, "gate") == "pass") "still passes" else
  paste("is", dm(unrel, "gate"))
```

The gate passes unless one of the `r nw(n_blockers)` blocking items fails:
falsifiability, which asks that some prediction be typed as a claim that rules a
result out, and the derivation chain, which asks that every prediction cite
declared propositions whose graph entails any claim it states. A file marked as
a draft makes the gate advisory. The gate's labels are the author's, so a file
can pass on a label: the second readers showed a prediction that 'motivated
people exist' opening the gate once it was labelled directional.

At f72ce4c, the derivation chain read claims as if the graph had no loops and
counted a claim it could not read as derived. Any feedback loop anywhere in the
propositions therefore switched off every claim check and could open a blocked
gate. The loops demonstrations show the change. A contradicted claim in an
acyclic graph scores `r sc(dm(acyc, "score"))` with the gate
`r dm(acyc, "gate")`. Adding a loop through the claim, or a loop between two
constructs unrelated to it, gave `r sc(dm(thru, "score", "old"))` and a passing
derivation chain at f72ce4c, and now gives `r loop_now`, with the item at
`r dm(unrel, "derivation_chain")`. An unread claim now earns no credit, but a
warning does not block, so under the default reading the gate `r gate_now`.
Reading the graph by sigma-separation (`check(cycles = "sigma")`) checks such
claims and blocks the gate when they fail, on the assumption that each loop
settles to a unique equilibrium.

The derivation chain checks agreement with the graph. It does not ask how far a
prediction goes beyond the propositions: a prediction that restates its one
proposition is entailed, and in the communication lens's count most of the
entailed verdicts in the shipped examples rest on a single proposition. Stating
a checkable claim can only expose an error and cost points, while leaving claims
out costs nothing, and a claim the graph cannot read now costs as much as a
contradicted one. The incentive the measurement lens described, to disclose
less, remains.

## Phenomena

At f72ce4c, a phenomenon whose claim the theory's own graph contradicts left
score and gate unchanged, while the same claim stated as a prediction blocked
the gate. Version `r pkg_version` fails the derivation chain for such a
phenomenon, so the gate is now
`r dm("phenomena/contradicted-phenomenon.theory.yaml", "gate")` in both cases.
The score still counts only predictions:
`r sc(dm("phenomena/contradicted-phenomenon.theory.yaml", "score"))` with the
contradicted phenomenon and
`r sc(dm("phenomena/contradicted-prediction.theory.yaml", "score"))` with the
contradicted prediction.

# The amendment appraisal {#sec-appraisal}

```{r}
#| label: appraisal-numbers
flip <- "amendments/sign-flip.theory.yaml"
weak <- "amendments/weakened-sign.theory.yaml"
prot <- "amendments/protects-only.theory.yaml"
app_rows <- vd$group == "Amendment appraisal"
```

`appraise_amendment()` compares two versions of a file and calls the amendment
progressive, degenerating or neutral by rules that borrow the terms of
@lakatos1970. At f72ce4c the rules compared implied independencies and stated
predictions but not the signs the two graphs entail. An amendment that reversed
the proposition behind a corroborated prediction, so that the new graph
contradicts it, was called `r dm(flip, "verdict", "old")`. Version
`r pkg_version` compares the signs as well. The same amendment is now
`r dm(flip, "verdict")`, with the prediction listed as content lost (the prior's
graph entails it and the new graph contradicts it) and the sign of the effect
listed as lost. An amendment that only weakens that sign to unsigned is
`r dm(weak, "verdict")` where it was `r dm(weak, "verdict", "old")`. An
assumption whose independent predictions are all untested is now classed as
pending rather than ad hoc, so a bold amendment is no longer called degenerating
before its prediction has been tested.

What remains is larger than what changed. The appraisal reads what the two files
declare and cannot check it. It cannot tell a prediction from an accommodation:
a subgroup re-description of the anomalous data, recorded as a new prediction
that passed, makes an amendment progressive, and so does an old result listed in
the 'protects' field of a trivial new assumption. The live run shows the second
case, `r dm(prot, "verdict")` with `r dm(prot, "protected_only")` reported as
new only through 'protects'. Whether a new prediction counts as new content or
as an articulation of old content depends on whether it states a
machine-readable claim. A single pass counts as corroboration whatever its
estimate, the severity of the test or the number of failed new predictions
beside it. Appraised one version at a time, a prediction made in one version and
corroborated in the next is never credited. And the appraisal has no notion of a
theory's hard core, so reversing its central claim can count as a progressive
problemshift.

Version `r pkg_version` reports several of these beside the verdict without
letting them decide it: the new predictions that count as new only through
'protects', the refuted new predictions and the lowest post-data severity of the
passes of each corroborated new prediction. The documents now say that the
verdict holds only if what the two files declare is true and that the rules
cannot tell a prediction from an accommodation. Of the `r nw(sum(app_rows))`
verdicts on the appraisal, the status register counts
`r status_phrase(vd$status[app_rows])`. A function that appraises a chain of
versions, fields for the provenance of data and a severity threshold for
corroboration are planned for 0.9.0. Even those would rest on the author's
declarations, so the most the appraisal can claim is conditional: if the
declarations are true, these rules give this verdict.

# The generated documents and the apps {#sec-outputs}

```{r}
#| label: outputs-numbers
doc_rows <- vd$group == "Documents and framing"
app_vrows <- vd$group == "Apps"
comm_f <- fd$lens == "communication-and-apps"
```

The preregistration, the dossier, the HTML report and the apps carry the
package's results to readers, and at f72ce4c they presented them as judgements.
The score was an 'aggregate rigour score' out of 100, the app said that the
checklist 'scores twelve facets of rigour', the dossier was called an audit,
'Derivations check: yes' headed preregistrations whose claims had not been read,
and the app coloured an entailed claim green and a rival's contradicted claim
red. The documentation's own scope sentence, that the score indexes how
completely a theory is specified and says nothing about whether it is true, was
accurate but appeared only on the methodology page and in the READMEs.

Version `r pkg_version` calls the number the checklist score wherever it is
shown, prints the same scope statement beside it in the help, the dossier, the
HTML report and the apps, opens the dossier with what is author-entered and what
is derived and the preregistration with what it holds and what must be added
before registration, takes the derivation line from the derivation chain read
with the document's own setting for loops, and uses neutral colours for the
causal readings and the rival comparison. Of the `r int(sum(comm_f))` findings
of the communication lens and its second reader, the status register counts
`r status_phrase(fd$status[comm_f])`. The two apps agree with each other and
with the packages. The lens's comparison of their displayed results found a
difference only in the help, which names the language.

Text beside a number may not change how it is read: automation bias occurs in
naive and expert users alike and cannot be prevented by training or instructions
[@parasuraman2010]. Moreover, every grading of a communication finding, the
lenses' and their second readers', is a judgement about likely misreading, not a
measurement of it. Study 3 of the protocol measures it.

# Dependence on the encoding {#sec-encoding}

```{r}
#| label: pilot-numbers
cbe <- rd("pilot/checklist_by_encoder.csv")
units <- rd("pilot/units_agreement.csv")
edges <- rd("pilot/edge_agreement.csv")
claims <- rd("pilot/claim_agreement.csv")
impl <- rd("pilot/implications_agreement.csv")
indep <- rd("pilot/independence_model_common.csv")
dsa <- rd("pilot/derived_sign_agreement.csv")
lin <- rd("pilot/linear_check.csv")
ichk <- rd("pilot/implications_independent_check.csv")
par <- rd("pilot/parity_r_python.csv")
prer <- rd("pilot/preregistration.csv")
pert <- rd("pilot/perturbations.csv")
summ <- fromJSON(file.path("data", "pilot", "summary.json"))
th_lab <- c("bilingual-rhm" = "RHM", "collaborative-cognitive-load" = "CCLT",
            "health-habit" = "habit")
n_enc <- length(unique(cbe$encoder))
n_th <- length(unique(cbe$theory))

u_all <- units[units$theory == "all", ]
u_k <- as.numeric(sub("/.*", "", u_all$all_three_same_element))
u_n <- as.numeric(sub(".*/", "", u_all$all_three_same_element))
u_ci <- wilson(u_k, u_n)
ed <- edges[edges$level == "directed" & edges$scope == "all", ]
lit <- unlist(impl[, grepl("^J_literal_basis", names(impl))])
habit_kappa <- indep$fleiss_kappa[indep$theory == "health-habit"]
reversals <- sum(dsa$sign_reversals)
ok_lists <- ichk[ichk$package == "ok", ]
n_lists <- nrow(ok_lists)
n_confirmed <- sum(ok_lists$n_confirmed)
lin_acyc <- lin[lin$criterion == "refuse", ]
lin_habit <- lin[lin$theory == "health-habit", ]
hyp_cclt <- prer$hypotheses[prer$theory == "collaborative-cognitive-load" &
                              prer$cycles == "refuse"]
habit_yes <- all(prer$derivations_check[prer$theory == "health-habit"] == "yes")
fill <- pert[startsWith(pert$perturbation, "1e"), ]
fill_after <- as.numeric(sub(".*aggregate: [0-9.]+ -> ([0-9.]+).*", "\\1", fill$changes))
icc_old <- icc1(cbe$aggregate, cbe$theory)
pl <- live[live$set == "pilot", ]
pl$theory <- sub("\\.theory\\.yaml$", "", basename(pl$file))
icc_new <- icc1(pl$score, pl$theory)
spread_old <- tapply(cbe$aggregate, cbe$theory, function(x) diff(range(x)))
spread_new <- tapply(pl$score, pl$theory, function(x) diff(range(x)))
theory_means_old <- tapply(cbe$aggregate, cbe$theory, mean)
old_pl <- old[old$set == "pilot", ]
n_invalid_pilot <- sum(old_pl$valid_full & !pl$valid_full)
n_pilot_files <- nrow(pl)
parity_text <- if (summ$parity_total_differences == 0) {
  "with no difference in any output compared"
} else paste("apart from", int(summ$parity_total_differences), "differences")
claims_text <- if (length(unique(claims$in_all_three)) == 1) {
  paste("only", nw(claims$in_all_three[1]), "in each case")
} else and_list(int(claims$in_all_three))
reversal_text <- if (reversals == 0) {
  "No derived sign ever reversed between encoders. The"
} else paste(Nw(reversals), "derived signs reversed between encoders, and most")
claims_union <- and_list(paste(int(claims$union), "for", th_lab[claims$theory]))
edges_common <- and_list(paste(int(ed$in_all_three), "of", int(ed$union), "for",
                               th_lab[ed$theory]))
spread_old_text <- and_list(paste(num(spread_old), "points for",
                                  th_lab[names(spread_old)]))
spread_new_text <- and_list(paste(num(spread_new), "points for",
                                  th_lab[names(spread_new)]))
```

Every output of the package describes a file, and a verbal theory can be written
into a file in more than one defensible way. The pilot measured how much this
matters with `r nw(n_enc)` encoders and `r nw(n_th)` theories.

The computations on each file were correct. The `r nw(n_pilot_files)` files gave
identical results in R and Python, `r parity_text`. A separation reader written
for the pilot, which does not use theoryforge, confirmed all
`r int(n_confirmed)` implied independencies in the `r int(n_lists)` lists the
package produced, and `r int(sum(lin_acyc$agree))` signs derived on the acyclic
files agreed with sampled linear models, with no exception.

The files differed. Of `r int(u_n)` source statements, `r int(u_k)` became the
same kind of element in every encoder's file (`r pct(u_k / u_n)`,
`r pct(ci_level)` interval from `r num(100 * u_ci[1], 0)` to `r pct(u_ci[2])`),
with Fleiss' kappa `r num(u_all$fleiss_fine, 2)` for the kind of element and
`r num(u_all$fleiss_claim, 2)` for whether a statement carries a claim the
package can check. Of the claims stated by any encoder (`r claims_union`), every
encoder stated `r claims_text`. Of the directed edges any encoder drew, every
encoder drew `r edges_common`. Literal agreement on the implied independencies,
as Jaccard indices between pairs of encoders, ranged from `r num(min(lit), 2)`
to `r num(max(lit), 2)`. Over the constructs that all the habit encoders used,
their independence models agreed less than chance would predict (Fleiss' kappa
`r num(habit_kappa, 2)`), because one choice the text leaves open, whether habit
prompts repetition directly or through behaviour, changes most of the
statements. `r reversal_text` disagreements were between zero and nonzero, or
between a fixed and an open sign. From the same text of collaborative cognitive
load theory the encoders produced `r and_list(int(hyp_cclt))` preregistered
hypotheses, because the format does not say when a stated relation should also
be a prediction.

Changing one element at a time traced each disagreement in the derivations to
ambiguity in the source text, to the format (an interaction encoded with the
'moderates' relation becomes an unsigned edge and leaves open a main effect the
theory states) or to the package's conservative reading of signs in loops of
more than one cycle, which left open
`r and_list(int(lin_habit$package_open_sampling_one_sign))` signs in the habit
files that every stable linear draw fixed.

The checklist scores of the encoders of one theory lay within
`r spread_old_text` at f72ce4c, and within `r spread_new_text` at
`r pkg_version`. That closeness says little about reliability. Most items were
the same in every file because the texts lack what they ask for, numbers,
measures, rivals and formal models, and the spread came almost entirely from
whether an encoder filled in the mechanism field. Filling the form without
changing any statement of a theory moved every file to between
`r sc(min(fill_after))` and `r sc(max(fill_after))`. The share of the variance
of the score that lay between theories, ICC(1), was `r num(icc_old["icc"], 2)`
at f72ce4c, with a `r pct(ci_level)` interval from `r num(icc_old["lower"], 2)`
to `r num(icc_old["upper"], 2)`, and is `r num(icc_new["icc"], 2)` (`r
num(icc_new["lower"], 2)` to `r num(icc_new["upper"], 2)`) at `r pkg_version`.
With `r nw(n_th)` theories the interval spans almost every possible value, so
the pilot cannot say whether the score separates theories at all. At
`r pkg_version`, `r nw(n_invalid_pilot)` of the files that passed full
validation at f72ce4c no longer do, because their encoders labelled a prediction
directional while its claim states no direction, which the release now refuses.

The pilot's limits are severe. The encoders were agents of one model family that
read the same documentation, the sources were short summaries by one author, and
one analyst matched the constructs. It says nothing about how far human
researchers would agree and gives no standard for whether any encoding is
faithful. What it does show is that the package's derivations can be trusted as
computations on a file, while the file is one of several defensible encodings,
and the scores and derivations describe the encoding rather than the theory.
Expert encoding does not remove the problem: when one research group encoded a
large set of behaviour-change theories, many of the encodings needed changes to
their constructs, their relations or both after feedback from the theories'
authors or other experts [@hale2020].

# What version `r pkg_version` changed {#sec-changes}

```{r}
#| label: status-numbers
crit_f <- fd$sev == "critical"
maj_f <- fd$sev == "major"
habit_files <- sort(live$file[grepl("health-habit", live$file)])
sigma_gate <- vapply(habit_files, function(f) {
  tf_check(tf_read(file.path("demonstrations", f)), cycles = "sigma")$gate
}, character(1))
names(sigma_gate) <- basename(dirname(habit_files))
refuse_gate <- live$gate[match(habit_files, live$file)]
sigma_text <- if (length(unique(sigma_gate)) == 1) {
  paste(unique(sigma_gate), "for all", nw(length(sigma_gate)), "habit files")
} else and_list(paste(sigma_gate, "for", names(sigma_gate)))
refuse_text <- if (all(refuse_gate == "pass")) "passes" else and_list(refuse_gate)
```

@tbl-status counts the status of every finding and verdict. Of the
`r int(n_find)` findings, `r int(nf("fixed"))` were fixed and
`r int(nf("reported"))` are now reported beside the result. Rewording met
`r int(nf("reworded"))`, while `r int(nf("unchanged"))` are unchanged and
`r int(nf("deferred"))` deferred. For the `r nw(n_crit)` critical findings the
counts are `r status_phrase(fd$status[crit_f])` (@tbl-critical), and for the
`r int(n_major)` major findings `r status_phrase(fd$status[maj_f])`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-status
#| tbl-cap: "Status in version 0.8.0 of every finding and verdict in the register."
stt <- data.frame(
  Status = status_order,
  Findings = sapply(status_order, function(s) sum(fd$status == s)),
  Verdicts = sapply(status_order, function(s) sum(vd$status == s)))
stt$All <- stt$Findings + stt$Verdicts
stt <- rbind(stt, data.frame(Status = "total", Findings = nrow(fd),
                             Verdicts = nrow(vd), All = nrow(fd) + nrow(vd)))
kab(stt)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-critical
#| tbl-cap: "The critical findings and their status in version 0.8.0."
ct <- fd[crit_f, c("id", "title", "status")]
ct$title <- sub("\\.$", "", ct$title)
kab(data.frame(Finding = ct$title, Status = ct$status))
```

@tbl-demos sets the demonstrations at f72ce4c beside the live run. Where a value
did not change, one value is shown.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demos
#| tbl-cap: "Demonstrations at f72ce4c and in the live run of version 0.8.0: score, gate and derivation chain, with 'a → b' where the value changed."
arrow <- function(a, b) ifelse(a == b, a, paste(a, "→", b))
dt <- data.frame(
  File = short(live$file),
  Score = arrow(sc(old$score), sc(live$score)),
  Gate = arrow(old$gate, live$gate),
  Chain = arrow(old$derivation_chain, live$derivation_chain))
kab(dt)
```

Some rules were corrected: the amendment appraisal reads signs and lost
entailments and has the pending class, a weakening is judged by the regions
rather than the labels, the derivation chain no longer counts unread claims and
reads phenomena, the preregistration and dossier take their derivation line from
the same reading of loops as their body, the rubric no longer rates a point
label without bounds as precise, and the simulation defaults to the exact
method. Some problems are now reported beside the result: the appraisal lists
novelty that rests on 'protects' alone, refuted new predictions and the
severities of the passes behind a progressive verdict, and the dossier flags a
recorded failure whose estimate lies inside its region. Most of the rest was
rewording, and it is substantial: every display now calls the number a checklist
score and says what it describes, the gate is described by what its blocking
items check, and the documents state the assumptions of the signs, what
'identified' means and what the simulation does not show.

What did not change matters more for the maintainer's question. The score still
rates empty, circular and refuted files highly and passes their gate, as
@tbl-demos shows. Apart from the derivation chain and the narrower rules above,
version `r pkg_version` changed what the score is called and what is said about
it, not what it computes. Declared severities still override the rubric, a rival
named without propositions still earns diagnosticity, labels still decide the
falsifiability blocker, and disclosing more still costs points. The appraisal
still cannot tell a prediction from an accommodation.

Rerunning the evidence on `r pkg_version` also showed one consequence of the new
rules that the register does not list. Under `check(cycles = "sigma")`, the
conservative reading of signs in loops of more than one cycle leaves open claims
that every stable linear model signs, and those claims now fail the derivation
chain. When this report was rendered, the gate under sigma-separation was
`r sigma_text`, while under the default reading their claims are not read and
the gate `r refuse_text`. A user who follows the preregistration's advice to
read loops by sigma-separation can thus see a theory blocked for claims that its
graph signs in every stable linear model.

# Is automated appraisal of theories feasible? {#sec-feasibility}

The evidence distinguishes deduction, description by fixed rules and appraisal.
Deduction from a stated graph can be computed soundly, and the package computes
it correctly within stated assumptions: what a set of causal propositions
implies about independencies and signs, what an adjustment can identify, which
directions data of a given kind cannot settle. This is deduction in a strict
sense, exact and checkable, and it is useful, because the implications of even a
small graph are easy to get wrong by hand.

A fixed rule can describe a file. It can say how completely a file states what a
checklist asks for, and it can apply declared outcomes consistently, as the
amendment appraisal does. Mechanical combination of information is not in itself
the weakness: across studies of human health and behaviour, mechanical
prediction was on average about as accurate as clinical prediction or more
[@grove2000], and human appraisals are not a perfect standard either, since
independent peer reviews of the same manuscript agree poorly [@bornmann2010].
The weakness lies in what the rules read. The checklist reads labels and the
presence of fields, which an author controls and which say nothing about whether
the theory is true. Summary scores of quality have behaved inconsistently in a
related field: in a meta-analysis of clinical trials, the conclusion changed
with the quality scale used to pick out the trials of high quality, and the
authors recommended assessing the relevant methodological aspects one by one
[@juni1999].

No part of the package has shown that it can judge a theory's quality, truth or
fruitfulness, or tell a prediction from an accommodation. Precedents for
computed appraisal exist. Explanatory coherence computes which of competing
hypotheses to accept from the explanatory relations a user encodes
[@thagard1989], and IMEC implements it as a model that psychologists can run in
R [@maier2024]. @meehl2002 proposed that a statistical composite of attributes
such as the number, diversity, novelty and numerical precision of the facts a
theory derives, and the number it misderives, could give an actuarial basis for
theory appraisal. Those attributes concern what a theory has derived and how its
derivations have fared. The checklist reads neither, and no rule of the package
has been calibrated against the later fate of theories, which an actuarial basis
of the kind Meehl proposed would need. The reasons why good psychological
theories are hard to develop that Eronen and Bringmann [-@eronen2021] give, the
scarcity of robust phenomena, the doubtful validity of constructs and the
difficulty of discovering causal relations between psychological variables,
arise before a theory is written into a file, and checking the file does not
address them.

So, as far as this evidence goes, automated appraisal of theories is feasible in
a narrow and conditional sense: the package can derive what an encoded theory
implies and describe how completely and consistently it is stated. It is not
feasible in the sense the maintainer doubted, of replacing a judgement of a
theory's merit, and nothing in the audit suggests that wording or weights would
make it so.

# What remains unvalidated {#sec-unvalidated}

```{r}
#| label: unvalidated-numbers
noval <- c("measurement-9", "metascience-and-related-tools-3", "pilot-10")
```

What has not been measured is how reliably different researchers encode the same
theory, whether the checklist and the appraisal agree with experts who judge the
same theories and amendments, and how readers read the outputs. The register's
findings on these (for example `r and_list(noval)`) are all
`r and_list(unique(fd$status[fd$id %in% noval]))`, because no study has been
run. `protocol.qmd` in this folder describes `r nw(n_studies)` preregistered
studies with human participants that would settle them. Study 1 measures how far
trained coders following a written protocol produce the same file from the same
published theory, at every level the package reads, beside human and agent
baselines. Study 2 compares the checklist and the appraisal with blind expert
ratings and tests whether known groups of corroborated, refuted and
pseudoscientific theories differ as they should. Study 3 is a randomised reader
study of how often researchers and editors misread the score, the gate, the
dossier and the appraisal in the 0.7.0 and 0.8.0 wording. A later cliometric
study would ask whether the outputs carry information about the later fate of
theories. Until such studies are reported, the outputs other than the deductions
should be read as descriptions of a file.

# Limitations of the audit {#sec-limits}

The audit has limits of its own, and they bear on its findings in both
directions.

All auditors, second readers and encoders were AI agents of one model family.
Their agreement may reflect shared training rather than independent
confirmation, and defects that all of them would miss are not in the register.
Where they judged how a reader would understand a display, they judged without
readers.

The audit examined one commit, and the status of 0.8.0 was established by
rerunning the audit's evidence, not by a new audit. Changes made in the release
were not themselves audited beyond those reruns, which is why the consequence of
the sigma reading in @sec-changes was found only now.

The lenses were chosen in advance. Others, such as an audit of security, of
accessibility or of the performance of the apps on large theories, were not part
of this audit.

Several positions were attributed to authors without their texts. The primary
texts of @lakatos1970, of Popper and of Mayo and Spanos [-@mayo2006] could not
be read, and the register marks where a verdict rests on the auditors' reasoning
or on secondary sources instead. This report attributes positions only to
sources whose abstracts or texts were read.

The demonstrations were built to probe what the score rewards. They were written
by agents who knew the checklist, the strong theories were encoded from short
source texts, and they are not a sample of real theories. They show what the
rules allow, not how often it happens.

There was no human comparison. Neither the checklist, nor the appraisal, nor the
encodings were compared with human judgement, so the audit cannot say how far
the package's outputs agree with experts, only that nothing in the package
establishes that they do.

```{r}
dd <- ver[!is.na(ver$discrepancies) & ver$discrepancies > 0, ]
kab(data.frame(Component = dd$component, Check = dd$quantity,
               Differ = paste(int(dd$discrepancies), "of", int(dd$cases))))
```
